picks.what_it_is: Astronomers measure the distances to very far galaxies with a 'standard ruler' left in the early universe (baryon acoustic oscillations). Turning a measurement into a distance needs an integral that a computer only approximates. Here a fast solver produced the numbers together with a table of whole-number checks, and the Lean proof checker then confirmed, step by step, that the true distance lies inside a narrow interval (relative width about 0.03%) at each of DESI's seven redshifts. Caveats: it is done at one value of the matter density, the project's own fit and not DESI's; it certifies a calculation, not a new measurement; the audit was by an AI agent, not a person.
picks.analogy_suggestion: A shop's till total re-added receipt by receipt by an auditor who trusts only pencil and paper.

picks.what_it_is: Two families of measurements of how fast the universe expands disagree (the 'Hubble tension'; the local, distance-ladder side sits near 73 km/s per megaparsec, the threshold this paper tests). Combining DESI distance data with what the first minutes of the universe tell us about light elements, this paper proves with Lean that, inside the standard flat model and its stated simplifications (radiation ignored, a fitting formula for the ruler, Gaussian errors), every expansion rate of 73 or more fits the data far worse than the best fit. It also certifies which matter densities are excluded. This is a certified version of a tension already known from ordinary statistics, not a new measurement; one pre-planned way of slicing the calculation failed and was replaced, and the paper says so.
picks.analogy_suggestion: Checking that a radio picks up no station anywhere on the dial above 73, band by band, with a notary signing each band.

picks.what_it_is: In September 2026 OpenAI released an AI-generated, computer-checked proof that, for a broad family of repulsive forces, the triangular arrangement has the lowest energy of all ways to place points on a plane at a given density. This paper derives consequences in Lean (for instance that the optimum is not unique: removing one point changes neither the density nor the energy), and checks one physical case, particles with a screened (Yukawa) repulsion, with an N-body simulation. Caveats, all stated: everything rests on the AI-generated upstream theorem, whose statement no person has audited; the simulation's cut-off of the force shifted energies by more than the gap being measured (an erratum fixed later in 10.5281/zenodo.23646105); simulated annealing failed to find the lattice at the weaker screening.
picks.analogy_suggestion: Oranges on a market stall: the proof says the neat stack is best; the simulation shakes the stall to see whether the oranges find it on their own.

picks.what_it_is: A batch of papers deposited on 19 October claimed, among other things, that a standard simulation method (RK4) slowly 'heats' charged particles in a fusion device's magnetic trap until they escape. Edition 2 tested that claim with 2,000 orbits per energy band and controls able to fail: the claim is false. At the step sizes used RK4 cools the particles, and its real failure is the opposite one: it traps particles that should escape. Confidence figures and a theorem from edition 1 were withdrawn, and the paper says no one but the author has reviewed it.
picks.analogy_suggestion: Blaming the thermostat for overheating the house, then measuring and finding that it keeps the house too cold.
picks.what_was_checked_and_how: Tier X experiment with a falsification rule fixed in advance and six passing controls; Lean results for the linear case (axiom footprint not stated in the record); no independent review.
picks.arc_phase: Phase 4 (Oct 17-21): relapse and withdrawal
picks.arc_role: Relapse and recovery: an over-claim from the 19 October batch withdrawn two days later by measuring it.
